title: Starting a Home Health Agency in Nebraska: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting a Home Health Agency (HHA) in Nebraska represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals needing skilled nursing, therapy, home health aide, and support services while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), which is responsible for both licensing and managing the state’s Medicaid program.

With strong state support, evidenced by the elimination of the Medicaid HCBS waitlist and an annual investment of approximately $45 million to expand these services, Nebraska offers a promising market for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. Reimbursement rates through Medicaid range from $25 to $75 per visit, creating a viable financial model for well-managed agencies. This environment makes Nebraska a promising market with strong state investment, particularly for providers targeting specialized niches or underserved rural areas.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Home Health Agency in Nebraska, from understanding the regulations and licensing process with the DHHS to staffing your team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for inspections. Whether you’re targeting urban centers like Omaha and Lincoln or addressing the needs of rural communities, this framework will help you build a foundation for success.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Nebraska’s Home Health Agency Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff

  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Nebraska’s Home Health Agency Regulations

Before you can serve a single patient, you must have a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape. Nebraska regulates Home Health Agencies through the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), which is responsible for the licensing and regulation of HHAs under the Health Care Facility Licensure Act (Sections 71-401 to 71-462). This body sets the standards for patient care, safety, staffing, and operational conduct.

Providers who intend to serve Medicare beneficiaries must also achieve federal certification by complying with the CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs). This is a separate, more intensive process that often occurs after state licensure. Additionally, all agencies must adhere to federal frameworks like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) to protect patient information.

The state’s regulatory framework emphasizes compliance with the Health Care Facility Licensure Act, focusing on patient care standards, safety, and documentation. This includes detailed requirements for patient rights, comprehensive assessments, care planning, service delivery, and clinical record-keeping. Licenses are not permanent; they typically require renewal annually, contingent on continued compliance and successful completion of any required surveys.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Not all home health agencies are the same. Nebraska’s market supports multiple service models and specializations, each with different operational, staffing, and reimbursement considerations. While a general HHA is a common starting point, focusing on a niche can create a competitive advantage.

Nebraska supports multiple Home Health Agency variants and specializations, including:

  • Skilled Nursing & Therapy Services: The traditional HHA model, providing registered nursing (RN), licensed practical nursing (LPN), physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) services.
  • Home Infusion/IV Therapy: A high-acuity niche focusing on administering intravenous medications, nutrition, and hydration in the patient’s home. This requires specialized nursing skills and pharmacy partnerships.
  • Pediatric Home Health: A specialized service line catering to the unique needs of children with complex medical conditions, often requiring ventilators, feeding tubes, and other advanced care.
  • Post-Acute Rehabilitation: Focusing on patients transitioning from a hospital or skilled nursing facility back to their homes. This service is therapy-intensive and built on strong relationships with hospital discharge planners.
  • HCBS Waiver Care Management: Providing skilled and unskilled services for individuals enrolled in Nebraska’s Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) waivers, such as those for the aged and disabled or individuals with developmental disabilities.

Program size is measured by patient census and staff capacity. While there’s no set limit, agencies must ensure their staffing levels can safely and effectively meet the needs of their clients. Demand is consistently strong in the urban centers of Douglas and Lancaster counties, though competition is also higher. In contrast, rural areas often have a moderate undersupply of providers, presenting a significant opportunity for new agencies willing to serve these communities.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing the correct legal and administrative foundation is a critical early step. Most providers in Nebraska choose to operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation to create a legal separation between the business and personal assets. Regardless of your choice, you must complete several key administrative tasks:

  • Register your business entity with the Nebraska Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and filing taxes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a complete licensing application to the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). This application is extensive and requires detailed information about your business structure, key personnel, proposed services, and operational policies.

The licensing process is not immediate. In Nebraska, licensing timelines generally range from 6 to 12 months, depending heavily on the completeness of your application, your readiness for the initial licensure survey, and the DHHS’s current processing times. Any errors or omissions in your application can cause significant delays.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a sustainable agency. It should include detailed financial projections based on realistic market data. In Nebraska, startup costs for a Home Health Agency typically range from $150,000 to $400,000. This capital covers licensing fees, legal and consulting costs, office setup, initial payroll, insurance, and the development of policies and procedures.

Your operating expenses will be driven primarily by your team. Staffing represents the largest ongoing cost, typically accounting for 50-60% of total expenses. Understanding your revenue streams is equally important. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Nebraska include:

  • Nebraska Medicaid: $25 – $75 per visit, depending on the discipline (e.g., skilled nursing vs. home health aide).
  • Medicare: Rates are determined by the Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM), which bases reimbursement on patient characteristics and care needs over a 30-day period.
  • Private Insurance/Managed Care: Rates are negotiated directly with each insurance company and are often higher than Medicaid but may come with complex authorization requirements.
  • Private Pay: Clients can pay out-of-pocket, with rates set by your agency based on market demand and service complexity.

With diligent management of referrals and staffing, providers operating at a target staff utilization of 70-80% can generally achieve gross margins in the 10-18% range. A well-executed business plan will project a break-even point within 12 to 18 months of operation.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

While care is delivered in the patient’s home, your agency must have a physical office that serves as your administrative hub. This location must be compliant with state regulations and professional standards. Key facility requirements include:

  • A secure, professional office space that is compliant with local zoning ordinances for commercial or medical businesses.
  • A designated, locked, and confidential area for storing patient records, whether they are physical charts or housed on a server. This is a critical HIPAA requirement.
  • Sufficient desk space for your Administrator, Director of Nursing, schedulers, and other administrative staff.
  • A secure and clean storage area for any medical supplies and equipment your agency maintains.
  • A HIPAA-compliant IT infrastructure, including secure computers, network, and Electronic Medical Record (EMR) software.

When selecting a location, consider more than just the rent. Your office should be accessible to your staff, centrally located within your desired service area, and present a professional image to referral sources and potential employees.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your agency. The quality of your care depends entirely on the team you build. Nebraska’s regulations mandate specific roles and qualifications to ensure patient safety and clinical oversight. Required roles for a Home Health Agency typically include:

  • Administrator/Director of Services: The individual responsible for the day-to-day operation of the agency and overall compliance.
  • Director of Nursing (DON) or Clinical Supervisor: A Registered Nurse (RN) who oversees all clinical services, supervises clinical staff, and ensures care plans are appropriate and followed.
  • Skilled Nurses (RNs and LPNs): To perform skilled assessments, treatments, and medication administration.
  • Therapists (PT, OT, SLP): If your agency offers rehabilitation services.
  • Home Health Aides (HHAs): Certified individuals who provide personal care and assistance with activities of daily living under the supervision of a nurse.
  • Office/Administrative Staff: To manage intake, scheduling, billing, and human resources.

Training is not a one-time event. State regulations require robust initial and ongoing training. This includes initial orientation covering agency policies, patient rights, and emergency procedures, as well as annual in-service training on critical topics like infection control, HIPAA, abuse prevention, and workplace safety. All clinical staff must undergo regular competency evaluations to ensure their skills remain sharp.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your agency cannot get licensed without a comprehensive set of policies and procedures. These documents are the operational playbook for your business, guiding every action from patient admission to billing. The DHHS will review these manuals in detail during your licensure survey. Nebraska requires written policies covering, at a minimum:

  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Patient Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Clinical Record and Documentation Standards
  • Infection Control and Exposure Plan
  • Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
  • Personnel Policies, Job Descriptions, and Credentialing
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program
  • Financial Management, Billing, and Collections

Beyond operational policies, the development and maintenance of individual care or service plans are central to compliance. Each patient must have a personalized plan of care, developed in coordination with their physician, that outlines their needs, goals, and the specific services your agency will provide. These plans must be regularly reviewed, updated, and meticulously documented to meet state and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike consumer products, home health services are not typically marketed through public advertising. Success depends on building strong, trust-based relationships with professional referral sources. Your marketing efforts should be strategic and targeted. In Nebraska, referrals for home health services typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Physician offices and specialty clinics (e.g., cardiology, orthopedics, oncology)
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)
  • Assisted Living Facilities and other senior living communities
  • Nebraska Medicaid HCBS waiver case managers
  • Geriatric care managers and elder law attorneys

Your reputation is your most powerful marketing tool. Successful providers differentiate themselves by focusing on rock-solid compliance, exceptional clinical outcomes, and responsive communication with referral sources. When a discharge planner knows your agency will respond quickly, admit the patient smoothly, and provide excellent care, they will call you first. Documenting your outcomes (e.g., low rehospitalization rates, improved patient function) provides concrete proof of your value.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Ongoing oversight is a permanent feature of operating a Home Health Agency. In Nebraska, oversight includes unannounced surveys conducted by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Licensure Unit. If your agency becomes Medicare-certified, you will also be subject to surveys from CMS or an approved accrediting organization (like CHAP or ACHC).

Inspectors focus on ensuring your agency is adhering to all state and federal regulations. Common deficiencies often cited during surveys include:

  • Incomplete, inconsistent, or outdated patient care plans.
  • Missing or late physician orders for care.
  • Inadequate supervision of Home Health Aides by a Registered Nurse.
  • Gaps in personnel files, such as expired licenses, missing background checks, or incomplete competency evaluations.
  • Breaches in infection control protocols.

To avoid these pitfalls, you must implement a robust Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) or QAPI program. This involves regularly auditing your own charts, processes, and outcomes to identify and correct issues before a surveyor finds them. Maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times is not just a best practice—it’s essential for survival.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Home Health Agency in Nebraska?

A: The entire process, from business planning and entity formation to accepting your first patient, typically takes 12 to 18 months. The state licensing application and survey portion alone can take 6-12 months of that time, so it’s critical to start with a complete and accurate application.

Q: What licenses are required to operate a Home Health Agency in Nebraska?

A: You must obtain a Home Health Agency license from the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). If you plan to serve Medicare beneficiaries, you will also need to achieve Medicare certification through a separate, rigorous process after you are state-licensed.

Q: What reimbursement is available for home health services in Nebraska?

A: Reimbursement comes from several sources. Nebraska Medicaid pays on a per-visit basis, ranging from approximately $25 to $75 depending on the service. Medicare uses the Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM), a complex system that pays for 30-day episodes of care. Other sources include private insurance companies and private pay from clients.

Conclusion

Starting a Home Health Agency in Nebraska is a challenging but immensely rewarding venture. The state’s commitment to expanding home and community-based services creates a favorable environment for new providers. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape governed by the DHHS, and unwavering operational discipline.

Providers who invest the time and resources to build a foundation of compliance, hire and train excellent staff, and cultivate strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and financial sustainability. By focusing on quality care and meticulous documentation, you can build an agency that not only thrives as a business but also makes a profound difference in the lives of Nebraskans.
